questions.question: Q1. Explain energy bands in solids.
questions.answer: In a solid, atoms are close that their atomic orbitals overlap into broad energy bands (valence band, conduction band) separated by a forbidden band gap E_g. Electrons can move in bands; they cannot have energies in the gap.
questions.shortcut: Close-packed atoms → orbitals merge into bands; gap in between.
questions.example: The gap size E_g decides the electrical type.

questions.question: Q2. Distinguish metals, insulators and semiconductors using band theory.
questions.answer: Metal: valence and conduction bands overlap (or partially filled) → electrons move freely (good conductor). Insulator: very large gap E_g (>3 eV) → few electrons in conduction band (poor conductor). Semiconductor: small gap E_g (~1 eV) → some conduction, sensitive to temperature.
questions.shortcut: Metal: bands overlap; Insulator: large E_g; Semiconductor: small E_g.
questions.example: Si (1.1 eV) is a semiconductor; glass is an insulator.

questions.question: Q3. Why does a semiconductor's conductivity increase with temperature?
questions.answer: Raising T excites more valence electrons across the small band gap into the conduction band, creating electron–hole pairs; more charge carriers mean higher conductivity (the opposite of a metal, whose carriers scatter more at high T).
questions.example: A sensor's resistance falls as it warms up.

questions.question: Q4. Define band gap and its effect on optical absorption.
questions.answer: The band gap E_g is the minimum energy to lift a valence electron into the conduction band. A material absorbs photons with hν ≥ E_g (and transmits/reflects the rest); larger E_g means absorption at shorter (bluer) wavelengths.
questions.shortcut: Absorb if hν ≥ E_g; larger gap → shorter wavelength.
questions.example: Diamond (E_g≈5.5 eV) is transparent in the visible.

questions.question: Q5. Explain why metals are shiny and good conductors.
questions.answer: A partially-filled band (or overlapping bands) leaves many free electrons that move under an applied field, giving high conductivity; the same electrons reflect incident light, so metals look shiny. ▥ 25.1–25.2 Energy Bands & Band Theory of Solids  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Conductor vs Semiconductor vs Insulator (band picture) Band Theory: What the Gap Controls ▣ 25.3 Intrinsic & Extrinsic Semiconductors
questions.example: Copper's free electrons make it both conductive and reflective.

questions.question: Q6. Define intrinsic semiconductor.
questions.answer: An intrinsic semiconductor is a pure semiconductor (e.g. Si, Ge) where the number of free electrons equals the number of holes (n₀ = p₀), both arising from thermal excitation across the gap; its resistivity is relatively high.
questions.shortcut: Pure: n = p (equal carriers); high resistivity.

questions.question: Q7. Explain extrinsic (doped) semiconductors: n-type and p-type.
questions.answer: Doping adds impurities: n-type uses a 5-valent donor (e.g. P in Si) adding extra electrons (majority carriers e⁻); p-type uses a 3-valent acceptor (e.g. B in Si) creating holes (majority carriers h⁺). Doping greatly increases conductivity.
questions.shortcut: n-type: donor (5-valent) → extra e⁻; p-type: acceptor (3-valent) → holes.
questions.example: P-doped Si is n-type; B-doped Si is p-type.

questions.question: Q8. Explain a p–n junction diode and its I–V behaviour.
questions.answer: Joining p- and n-type forms a depletion layer and a built-in potential. Forward bias (p +ve) reduces the barrier, allowing current after ~0.7 V (Si); reverse bias widens the barrier, blocking current until breakdown. The I–V curve is asymmetric (rectifier).
questions.shortcut: Forward: ~0.7 V (Si) conducts; Reverse: blocks (except breakdown).
questions.example: A diode lets current one way only.

questions.question: Q9. What is an electron–hole recombination and where is it used?
questions.answer: A conduction-band electron falls into a valence-band hole, annihilating both carriers (may emit light in a direct-gap semiconductor). Recombination is the working principle of an LED (light emitted) and of charge storage in a solar cell when separated.
questions.shortcut: e⁻ + h⁺ → recombine (may emit a photon).
questions.example: An LED glows when carriers recombine.

questions.question: Q10. Compare the effect of doping on the Fermi level.
questions.answer: In an intrinsic semiconductor the Fermi level is near mid-gap. Doping shifts it: n-type moves it toward the conduction band (more e⁻); p-type moves it toward the valence band (more h⁺), reflecting the dominant carrier type.
questions.shortcut: n-type: Fermi ↑ (toward C); p-type: Fermi ↓ (toward V).
questions.example: The Fermi position tells the majority carrier.

questions.question: Q11. Explain the use of semiconductors in a solar cell.
questions.answer: A p–n junction solar cell absorbs sunlight, generating electron–hole pairs; the junction's built-in field separates them, producing a photocurrent and voltage. Connecting many cells in series gives a usable DC voltage for power. ▥ 25.3 Intrinsic & Extrinsic Semiconductors  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Semiconductor n-type vs p-type Semiconductor PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: Light → e⁻–h⁺ pairs → junction separates them → current.
questions.example: Rooftop PV panels are arrays of p–n solar cells.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T1. Compare the conduction in metals, insulators and semiconductors, including temperature effects.
theoryItems.answer: Metal: many free electrons; conductivity falls slightly with temperature (more scattering). Insulator: large gap, negligible conduction. Semiconductor: small gap; conductivity rises strongly with temperature (more e⁻–h⁺ pairs), the opposite of a metal.
theoryItems.shortcut: Metal: T↑ σ↓ ; Insulator: insulates ; Semiconductor: T↑ σ↑.
theoryItems.example: A sensor's resistance falls as it warms up.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T2. Explain the band theory of solids and how orbitals form bands.
theoryItems.answer: In a solid, atoms are close that their atomic orbitals overlap and broaden into energy bands (valence band, conduction band) separated by a forbidden band gap E_g. Electrons can occupy bands; they cannot have energies in the gap. The band structure (filling and gap size) determines the electrical type.
theoryItems.shortcut: Close atoms → orbitals merge into bands; gap between V and C.
theoryItems.example: The gap size E_g sets the material type.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T3. Explain the energy-band structure of a metal and why it conducts.
theoryItems.answer: In a metal, the valence and conduction bands overlap (or the band is only partially filled), so there are free electrons that can move under a small applied field, giving high conductivity. The same free electrons reflect light, making metals shiny.
theoryItems.shortcut: Metal: bands overlap/partially filled → free e⁻ → conductive.
theoryItems.example: Copper's free electrons make it both conductive and reflective.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T4. Explain the band structure of an insulator and why it does not conduct.
theoryItems.answer: In an insulator, the valence band is full and the conduction band empty, separated by a large band gap (E_g > ~3 eV). At room temperature very few electrons have enough energy to cross the gap, so there are almost no carriers and it does not conduct.
theoryItems.shortcut: Insulator: large E_g (>3 eV) → few carriers.
theoryItems.example: Glass, rubber, plastic have large gaps → insulators.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain the band structure of a semiconductor and intrinsic conduction.
theoryItems.answer: A semiconductor has a small band gap (~1 eV for Si). At room temperature some valence electrons thermally cross into the conduction band, creating a free electron and a hole; the conductivity rises with temperature. In an intrinsic (pure) semiconductor, n = p (equal electrons and holes).
theoryItems.shortcut: Semiconductor: small E_g (~1 eV); n = p intrinsic.
theoryItems.example: Si (1.1 eV) conducts a little at room temperature.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain n-type and p-type (extrinsic) semiconductors by doping.
theoryItems.answer: Doping adds impurities: n-type uses a 5-valent donor (e.g. P in Si) adding extra conduction electrons (majority carriers e⁻); p-type uses a 3-valent acceptor (e.g. B in Si) creating holes (majority carriers h⁺). Doping greatly increases the conductivity.
theoryItems.shortcut: n-type: donor → e⁻ ; p-type: acceptor → h⁺.
theoryItems.example: P-doped Si is n-type; B-doped Si is p-type.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain a p–n junction diode and its forward/reverse behaviour.
theoryItems.answer: Joining p- and n-type forms a depletion layer and a built-in potential. Forward bias (p positive) reduces the barrier, allowing current after ~0.7 V (Si); reverse bias widens the barrier, blocking current until breakdown. The asymmetric I–V makes it a rectifier.
theoryItems.example: A diode conducts one way only.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain how a solar cell converts light to electricity.
theoryItems.answer: A p–n junction solar cell absorbs sunlight, generating electron–hole pairs; the junction's built-in field separates them, pulling electrons to the n-side and holes to the p-side, producing a photocurrent and a voltage. Connecting many cells in series gives a usable DC voltage for power.
theoryItems.shortcut: Light → e⁻–h⁺ pairs → junction separates them → current.
theoryItems.example: Rooftop PV panels are arrays of p–n solar cells.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T9. Explain an LED and the role of band gap in its colour.
theoryItems.answer: An LED is a forward-biased p–n junction; when an electron in the conduction band recombines with a hole in the valence band, it emits a photon of energy hν ≈ E_g, so the colour (wavelength) is set by the band gap. A larger E_g gives a bluer (shorter) wavelength.
theoryItems.example: A 1.6 eV LED emits red; a 3 eV LED emits blue/UV.

theoryItems.question: [Viva] T10. Professor: 'What is a hole and how does it behave as a charge carrier?'
theoryItems.answer: A hole is the absence of an electron in a filled valence band; when a neighbouring electron fills it, the hole 'moves' the other way, behaving as a positive charge carrier. It is not a real particle but a useful way to describe positive current flow in a semiconductor.
theoryItems.shortcut: Hole = absence of e⁻, acts like + charge.
theoryItems.example: In p-type, holes are the majority carriers.

theoryItems.question: [Numerical] T11. An LED uses a semiconductor with E_g = 2.0 eV. Estimate its emission wavelength.
theoryItems.answer: hν ≈ E_g → λ = hc/E_g = (1240 eV·nm)/2.0 eV ≈ 620 nm (red light).

formulas: Energy bands: valence (V), conduction (C), gap E_g between them.
Metal: V & C overlap/merged; Insulator: E_g large (>~3 eV); Semiconductor: E_g small (~1 eV).
Intrinsic: equal e⁻ & h⁺ ; Doping: n-type (donor, e⁻ rich), p-type (acceptor, h⁺ rich).

▣ 25.1–25.2 Energy Bands & Band Theory of Solids
Q1. Explain energy bands in solids.

Answer:  In a solid, atoms are close that their atomic orbitals overlap into broad energy bands (valence band, conduction band) separated by a forbidden band gap E_g. Electrons can move in bands; they cannot have energies in the gap.
⚡ Shortcut:  Close-packed atoms → orbitals merge into bands; gap in between.
Example:  The gap size E_g decides the electrical type.
Q2. Distinguish metals, insulators and semiconductors using band theory.

Answer:  Metal: valence and conduction bands overlap (or partially filled) → electrons move freely (good conductor). Insulator: very large gap E_g (>3 eV) → few electrons in conduction band (poor conductor). Semiconductor: small gap E_g (~1 eV) → some conduction, sensitive to temperature.
⚡ Shortcut:  Metal: bands overlap; Insulator: large E_g; Semiconductor: small E_g.
Example:  Si (1.1 eV) is a semiconductor; glass is an insulator.
Q3. Why does a semiconductor's conductivity increase with temperature?

Answer:  Raising T excites more valence electrons across the small band gap into the conduction band, creating electron–hole pairs; more charge carriers mean higher conductivity (the opposite of a metal, whose carriers scatter more at high T).
⚡ Shortcut:  T ↑ → more e⁻–h⁺ pairs → σ ↑ (semiconductors).
Example:  A sensor's resistance falls as it warms up.
Q4. Define band gap and its effect on optical absorption.

Answer:  The band gap E_g is the minimum energy to lift a valence electron into the conduction band. A material absorbs photons with hν ≥ E_g (and transmits/reflects the rest); larger E_g means absorption at shorter (bluer) wavelengths.
⚡ Shortcut:  Absorb if hν ≥ E_g; larger gap → shorter wavelength.
Example:  Diamond (E_g≈5.5 eV) is transparent in the visible.
Q5. Explain why metals are shiny and good conductors.

Answer:  A partially-filled band (or overlapping bands) leaves many free electrons that move under an applied field, giving high conductivity; the same electrons reflect incident light, so metals look shiny.
⚡ Shortcut:  Free electrons → conduction + reflection (shine).
Example:  Copper's free electrons make it both conductive and reflective.

▣ 25.3 Intrinsic & Extrinsic Semiconductors
Q6. Define intrinsic semiconductor.

Answer:  An intrinsic semiconductor is a pure semiconductor (e.g. Si, Ge) where the number of free electrons equals the number of holes (n₀ = p₀), both arising from thermal excitation across the gap; its resistivity is relatively high.
⚡ Shortcut:  Pure: n = p (equal carriers); high resistivity.
Example:  Pure silicon at room temperature.
Q7. Explain extrinsic (doped) semiconductors: n-type and p-type.

Answer:  Doping adds impurities: n-type uses a 5-valent donor (e.g. P in Si) adding extra electrons (majority carriers e⁻); p-type uses a 3-valent acceptor (e.g. B in Si) creating holes (majority carriers h⁺). Doping greatly increases conductivity.
⚡ Shortcut:  n-type: donor (5-valent) → extra e⁻; p-type: acceptor (3-valent) → holes.
Example:  P-doped Si is n-type; B-doped Si is p-type.
Q8. Explain a p–n junction diode and its I–V behaviour.

Answer:  Joining p- and n-type forms a depletion layer and a built-in potential. Forward bias (p +ve) reduces the barrier, allowing current after ~0.7 V (Si); reverse bias widens the barrier, blocking current until breakdown. The I–V curve is asymmetric (rectifier).
⚡ Shortcut:  Forward: ~0.7 V (Si) conducts; Reverse: blocks (except breakdown).
Example:  A diode lets current one way only.
Q9. What is an electron–hole recombination and where is it used?

Answer:  A conduction-band electron falls into a valence-band hole, annihilating both carriers (may emit light in a direct-gap semiconductor). Recombination is the working principle of an LED (light emitted) and of charge storage in a solar cell when separated.
⚡ Shortcut:  e⁻ + h⁺ → recombine (may emit a photon).
Example:  An LED glows when carriers recombine.
Q10. Compare the effect of doping on the Fermi level.

Answer:  In an intrinsic semiconductor the Fermi level is near mid-gap. Doping shifts it: n-type moves it toward the conduction band (more e⁻); p-type moves it toward the valence band (more h⁺), reflecting the dominant carrier type.
⚡ Shortcut:  n-type: Fermi ↑ (toward C); p-type: Fermi ↓ (toward V).
Example:  The Fermi position tells the majority carrier.
Q11. Explain the use of semiconductors in a solar cell.

Answer:  A p–n junction solar cell absorbs sunlight, generating electron–hole pairs; the junction's built-in field separates them, producing a photocurrent and voltage. Connecting many cells in series gives a usable DC voltage for power.
⚡ Shortcut:  Light → e⁻–h⁺ pairs → junction separates them → current.
Example:  Rooftop PV panels are arrays of p–n solar cells.
